items.title: Hannah Otto Broke Her Leg Descending Kilimanjaro—and Kept Riding
items.summary:
By the time professional mountain biker Hannah Otto, 30, reached the final miles of her descent from Mount Kilimanjaro, 19,341 feet, she had already navigated the mountain’s most punishing terrain. She’d hauled her bike up snowy slopes, scrambled over boulders at 18,000 feet, and ridden steep, rocky trails where softball-sized stones shifted beneath her tires. Now she was on a rainforest dirt road easy enough to ride on a gravel bike.

On November 3, Otto became the first known woman to ascend and descend Africa’s tallest mountain with a bicycle in a single day. She completed the effort in 10 hours, 18 minutes, and 51 seconds, despite breaking her leg just two miles from the finish.

“I came around a gentle bend in the trail, and the trail went from dry dirt to mud, and it was like I hit ice,” Otto told Outside. “The bike just came out from underneath me, and I was on the ground in a second.”

The fall had broken her leg. But two miles from the finish, she got back on her bike and rode out.

The attempt was also part of a fundraising campaign for World Bicycle Relief , a nonprofit that provides bicycles to improve access to education, healthcare, and employment. Otto hopes to raise $165,000 to provide 1,000 bicycles to rural African communities.

Otto carries her mountain bike across a snow-covered section of Kilimanjaro. The upper slopes were too steep to ride, forcing her to carry the bike for roughly three miles.

items.title: Under-the-Radar Overlanding Spots in the West, According to a Full-Timer
items.summary:
There is a specific moment, usually about ten or twenty miles after the asphalt dissolves into dirt, when the noise of the modern world begins to cut out completely. The cell bars drop to zero, the tourist traffic vanishes in your rearview mirror, and the real adventure begins. But planning a camping trip these days feels almost like buying concert tickets. You wait months for a release date, log onto a park website, fight for a reservation, and ultimately end up with your tent pitched a few feet from an RV, falling asleep to the soul-soothing sound of their generator howling through the night.

Even as a full-time overlander , I’d love to say I gave up on the asphalt lottery long ago, but sadly, for some places, it’s the only way left to experience them. True wilderness is still out there, though. Finding it just means trading the pavement for dirt tracks and exploration.

The author’s custom-built Jeep Rubicon overland rig on the road. (Photo: Jay Clue) 
 While social media loves to showcase six-figure custom trucks wrapped in tactical gear, crawling through hood-deep mud or hanging off thousand-foot cliffs, the real secret to overlanding isn’t in the extremes. It’s about finding your own beautiful piece of serenity in the backcountry. At its heart, overlanding is simply vehicle-based travel. In other words, using your rig as a mobile backpack to carry your kitchen, bed, and gear deeper into the wild than any paved road could ever take you. You don’t need a custom-built rock crawler or axle-breaking trails. All you need is a dirt track, a map, and your sense of…
items.t: Under-the-Radar Overlanding Spots in the West, According to a Full-Timer

items.title: Finally, Data on Super-High Carbohydrate Doses
items.summary:
Science often moves very slowly. But sometimes, when the real-world stakes are high enough, it zips along at an impressive pace. That’s what’s currently happening with carbohydrate fueling for endurance sports. It’s a hot topic with lots of open questions, and a big new study offers some useful—though not entirely final —answers.

Over the last half-dozen years, top cyclists, runners, triathletes, and others have been pushing back the limits of what was thought possible. The existing science said you couldn’t make use of more than 90 grams of carbohydrate per hour, but elite athletes are now routinely using 120 grams per hour and, in some cases, far beyond that. At last year’s New York Marathon, Joe Klecker reportedly downed 175 grams per hour—the sports gel equivalent of eating nine servings of cooked pasta during the race .

Whether these carb megadoses actually improve performance is a different question. So far, the research has been equivocal . And critics like the South African sports scientist Tim Noakes have claimed that big carb doses don’t help at all, at least as a source of fuel for your muscles. Noakes argues that a mere 10 grams an hour is enough to keep your blood sugar from crashing, which in his view is all that matters.

When I wrote about this debate last year, I thought it would be straightforward to dig up “dose-response” data showing what dose of carbs led to the best endurance performances. To my surprise, though, the existing evidence was sparser than I expected. What we needed, I concluded, was fresh dose-response data spanning the whole range from…

items.title: I’ve Been a Night Owl All My Life. Here Are 7 Things I Did to Become a Morning Exerciser.
items.summary:
I am a consummate night owl. When I was a teenager, my mother used to begin waking me up by knocking on my door, then taking my pillow away, then my bed sheets. When she’d find me still asleep on the bare mattress, she’d push me onto the floor. That’s where my little brother would find me, still asleep, and begin wailing that I needed to drive him to school because he didn’t want to be late (again).

Waking up in the morning has never been my strong suit. But when I graduated from college and no longer had a coach holding me to a daily afternoon cross-country practice, I found that exercise stopped being a priority. By the time I got off work at 5 p.m., I was too tired to go to the gym, or I had dinner plans, or had eaten something weird and decided it was impossible to run.

For weeks at a time, exercise just wouldn’t happen. Certain that turning myself into a morning exerciser would solve all my problems, I told my mom I was on a mission to become an early bird. She shook her head. “I’ve been trying my whole life,” she said. “If you figure it out, you let me know.”

Most folks consider the night-owl versus early-bird categorization a matter of intrinsic wiring—you’re born one or the other, and you cannot change. While there is a strong genetic basis for your natural circadian rhythm, it is possible to switch . In fact, after about a year of working to adjust my sleep cycle, I now wake up at or before 6 a.m. almost every morning (even when I don’t necessarily want to). That means I now get to the gym or trail four or five days a week instead of one or two. Here are all…
items.t: I’ve Been a Night Owl All My Life. Here Are 7 Things I Did to Become a Morning Exerciser.

items.title: Giant November Waves Threaten Surfers, Swimmers, and Spectators Along California’s Coast
items.summary:
Lifeguards along California’s coast have had their hands full over the past several days, as powerful Pacific swells stranded surfers, swept a teenager photographing the waves off rocks, and even overturned a rescue jet ski during an operation near Santa Cruz.

In San Diego alone, lifeguards conducted 175 water rescues between November 9 and 16, according to San Diego Fire-Rescue figures reported by FOX 5/KUSI .

“I’ve seen seasons start off with a bang like this, but we’ve never had this type of impact so immediate,” Ernst Bauen, operations division chief for the Central Fire District of Santa Cruz County, told Outside on November 17.

The enormous swells were generated by powerful low-pressure systems over the northeastern Pacific, where hurricane-force winds pushed waves toward the California coast, according to the National Weather Service. On November 14, forecasters predicted breaking waves of 25 to 35 feet, with occasional sets reaching 40 to 50 feet at big-wave surfing spot  Mavericks , near Half Moon Bay.

Bauen, who spent about 20 years as a rescue swimmer, said waves are reaching roads, cliffs, and beach access points earlier in the season than usual.

“The ocean is extremely dynamic, and where there used to be a safe amount of space to recreate even on the beach, those spaces are becoming fewer and further between because of the erosion along our coastline,” he said.

items.title: Lawmakers Move to Ban AI Data Centers on National Forests and Federal Land
items.summary:
There’s a new plan in Washington to prohibit the construction of AI data centers on public lands.

On November 11, Oregon Representative Maxine Dexter introduced the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act , which would ban new data centers on national forests and lands managed by the U.S. Department of the Interior.

The legislation, backed by 13 Democratic cosponsors, would also require federal land sold or transferred to return to government ownership if used for a data center without congressional authorization.

“Public lands belong in public hands and Oregonians must have a say before the federal government hands over millions of acres of public land managed by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) for data centers,” Dexter said in a November 11 press release . “These treasured lands are where people hunt, fish, hike and graze livestock. They are where wildlife habitat and our critical watersheds are protected. My bill keeps these lands safe from data centers now, and for the generations who come after us.”

The bill arrived just one day after the Interior Department published its strategic plan for fiscal years 2026 through 2030 , which outlines proposals to sell federal land to states, local governments, and tribes, while expanding energy and infrastructure development to support growing demand from data centers.

The plan drew criticism from public lands advocates, including Tracy Stone-Manning, who led the BLM under President Joe Biden and now serves as president of the Wilderness Society.

items.title: Editor’s Letter: Why Do Hard Things Outside? Our Outsiders of the Year Answer
items.summary:
“But why?”

Anyone who does hard things outside has heard it. Why climb a mountain that’s already been climbed? Why run 253 miles across a desert? To test the limits of human potential is the tidy answer. The real one, as our Outsiders of the Year show, shifts like snow on a big face: it’s different for everyone, and never quite the same twice.

This year Alex Honnold free soloed a 1,667-foot skyscraper live on Netflix, after being explained away as a brain-scan curiosity for two decades. Now 40, with two preschoolers, he fits climbing in where he can. Some days that means getting up at 2 a.m. to climb a thousand-foot granite wall to still make it home for dinner. Why bother? “In some ways, climbing is my only opportunity to feel like I’m good at something,” he tells Features Editor Frederick Dreier. Any parent who has squeezed in a run between school pickups knows the feeling.

Jim Morrison and his partner Hilaree Nelson shared a dream no one had pulled off: to climb Everest’s North Face and ski it back down. In 2022, Nelson died on Manaslu, and Morrison swore off the mountains. Then his dog started pulling him back up the trail, a little higher every day. In 2025, with Jimmy Chin filming beside him for Everest: The Other Side , Morrison skied 9,000 feet off the top of the world. At the bottom, he screamed, “That one’s for you, Hil.”

Not everyone on Everest gets to ask why. Sherpas still take the biggest risks so others can reach the top. This spring, Hillary Dawa Sherpa , a 57-year-old cook, was pushed toward the summit when his outfitter came up a guide short.…
items.t: Editor’s Letter: Why Do Hard Things Outside? Our Outsiders of the Year Answer
